S.1 Specimen Information

S.1.1 Field Sampling

Grutas Tzabnah, which means "King's Palace" in Maya, is located 40 km SE of Mérida near
the town of Tecoh, Yucatán, Mexico. The Tzab06-1 speleothem was collected in 2006. With
consideration of cave conservation, the analysed stalagmite was selected from previously
broken and harvested material. The most probable stalagmite base was identified during
fieldwork in 2022. This sample location is in a large chamber ("Dome of the Cathedral")
located ~425 m from the entrance, beneath ~7 m of overburden, and contains both standing
water (Cenote 10) and a small artificial well (La Noria) in the chamber ceiling, constructed in
the Colonial Period (fig. S6).

Initial lower-resolution δ18O and U/Th analysis was conducted on Tzab06-1 in 2007 to
identify its palaeoclimate utility. Those preliminary data are not presented, and all U/Th and
stable isotope data herein were collected in 2021 and 2022. The sampled section of Tzab06-1
was stored at room temperature at the University of Florida and University of Cambridge
between 2006 and recent analysis starting in 2021.

S.1.2 Provenance

Tzab06-1 was retrieved from Grutas Tzabnah by the cave’s custodians before 2006 and gifted
to David A. Hodell in 2006 in collaboration with representatives from Tecoh’s local
government, which owns and manages the cave, and with permission from the Instituto
Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH). As part of this study, Tzab06-1 was validated
for authenticity by replication with another stalagmite from the same cave (Chaac) and dated

S.2 Local Climate and Stable Isotopes of Rain

At Grutas Tzabnah (Fig. 3) and Río Secreto (fig. S7), the oxygen isotope ratio of rainwater
(δ18Orw) captures the annual cycle of rainfall amount, with more negative values in the wet
season (boreal summer) and less negative values in the dry season (boreal winter). This
demonstrates the ability of δ18Orw in the northern Yucatán region to record seasonal cyclicity,
though (palaeo)climate evidently varies on a local scale, such as between Grutas Tzabnah and
Río Secreto.

The multi-year climate dataset at Río Secreto recorded the local meteorological wet-season
drought year of 2016 (May-October 2016 rainfall was 466 mm, versus that at the nearby
Playa del Carmen meteorological station, with a long-term average of 950 mm), with
amount-weighted summer δ18Orw -2.7 ‰ (VSMOW), compared with the previous two years,
which had amount-weighted summer δ18Orw values of -5.0 ‰ and -5.3 ‰ VSMOW (35,36)

(fig. S7). We expect that Grutas Tzabnah will be able to record seasonal drought in the same
way, when multi-year monitoring data become available.


S.3 Stable Isotopes of Dripwater

The single year of monitoring data at Grutas Tzabnah indicate that the seasonal signal in
δ18Orw is reliably transferred to the oxygen isotope ratio of dripwater (δ18Odw). Fig. 3 (main
text) shows the single full year of data, which displays a distinct seasonal cycle with lower
δ18Odw during the wet season and higher δ18Odw during the dry season, like the δ18Orw signal.
This seasonality is also apparent in δD and D-excess (fig. S8). These data confirm our
assertion that the thin (~7 m) karst overburden atop Grutas Tzabnah does not cause a
reservoir-effect sufficient to eliminate the seasonal δ18Orw signal, although the amplitude of
intra-annual variability is damped.

Direct comparison of rainfall amount and δ18Odw reveals inheritance of monthly-scale
variation in rainfall amount by δ18Odw, with an offset of one month, to the nearest month,
(Fig. 3, main text). Comparison of δ18Odw and δ18Orw corroborates this: regression between
the two measures with no offset yields R2 = 0.23, a one month offset increases the regression
to R2 = 0.51, a two-month offset then decreases it to R2 = 0.03, and >2 months produces a
negative correlation.

S.5 Comparison to other records

S.5.1 Palaeoclimate Proxy Records

In comparing Tzab06-1 to other palaeoclimate records from the region (Fig. 4, main text), we
prioritised the chronology of Tzab06-1, given its smaller uncertainty. For comparison, Chaac
was shifted forward by two years, well within the stated uncertainty of the record (15) (±10).
No alterations were made to the chronology of the southern Belize Yok-I speleothem (16).

The additional local speleothem record VP-10-01 (26,86) displays the same variability as the
Chaac record, but with lower resolution and chronological certainty. It therefore also
corroborates the results from Tzab06-1 (fig. S9).

Sufficiently long meteorological droughts can lower water tables and affect the hydrologic
budgets of lakes. Gypsum horizons in sediment profiles from Lake Chichancanab, north-
central Yucatán Peninsula, are indicative of hydrologic drought, i.e., times when evaporation
exceeds precipitation for multiple consecutive years, given that the residence time of lake
water is significantly longer than an annual cycle (87). This results in lake-level lowering and
supersaturation of the lake water with respect to gypsum (13,87). We hypothesise that the ≥3-
year extreme droughts recorded as δ18Occ excursions in the Tzab06-1 speleothem reflect
meteorological drought events of sufficient intensity to induce hydrological drought.

The chronology of the Chichancanab gypsum record is poorly resolved compared to that of
Tzab06-1, given the relatively large errors of the 14C dates on samples from the lake sediment
core. Dates that constrain gypsum deposition have errors on calendar dates that average ±120
years (95 % confidence interval). Additionally, the age model assumes linear interpolation

between each 14C tie-point, without accounting for likely different accumulation rates of the
interbedded gypsum and organic-rich sediment (gyttja). Although the radiocarbon
chronologies of Lake Chichancanab sediment cores are not precise enough to prove temporal
correlation between the multi-year droughts recorded in Tzab06-1 and gypsum layers found
in the lake, patterns between the two records are similar, under the assumption that only
extreme droughts are of sufficient intensity and duration to induce hydrological drought (fig.
S9). The four multi-year droughts observed between 889 and 938 CE correspond to a set of
gypsum peaks in the lake sediment record. Longer droughts (889-894 CE, 895-901 CE, and
925-938 CE) induced thicker gypsum layers, interposed by a thinner layer that might reflect
the shorter drought of 908-912 CE, suggesting that the single wet year between the droughts
of 889-894 CE and 895-901 CE would not have been sufficient to end the hydrological
drought. The later set of gypsum horizons that overlie this initial set may therefore
correspond to the ‘Postclassic Megadrought’ in the YOK-I speleothem (16) and the hiatus in
Tzab06-1, though the cause of drip cessation at that time is unclear and may not have been
associated with dry conditions in Grutas Tzabnah.

S.6 Additional Proxies

Carbon isotopes (δ13C) in speleothems can be influenced by changes in climate but also
respond to a subset of associated factors. The primary source of carbon to a karst drip is
dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) from respiration in the overlying soil, and as such, δ13C
values reflect the source of organic matter in soil (C3 vs C4 vegetation) and microbial
activity in the soil (88). In a stable location that is not affected by substantial changes in
vegetation type, more productive soils should result in lower DIC δ13C values in soil water, a
correlation that has been used regionally to reconstruct climate (27,89,90). In this sense, DIC
δ13C values in soil water covary with δ18Odw to a degree because the soil is less productive
during more arid periods and responds to the seasonal rainfall cycle. We thus would expect to
see pronounced seasonality in the speleothem δ13Ccc record, and long-term (decadal-scale)
shifts in response to prolonged droughts. Longer droughts would be expected to cause greater
soil degradation, as soils cannot be replenished over many consecutive muted wet seasons, as
opposed to a single dry year or droughts of only 2-3-year duration. δ13Ccc also responds to
calcite precipitation in air-filled voids along the drip pathway in the karst (prior calcite
precipitation, PCP). With such a thin overburden, the effect of PCP at Grutas Tzabnah is
thought to be minimal (see below).

Seasonal cyclicity in Tzab06-1 is more pronounced for δ13Ccc than for δ18Occ (fig. S1), with
clear maxima and minima visible even during periods of suppressed annual extremes in the
δ18Occ signal. On a decadal scale, three positive δ13Ccc excursions are apparent: c. 880-900
CE, c. 925-945 CE, and c. 970-990 CE. Between c. 970 and 990 CE, the frequency of
shorter-duration (1-2 year) dry events appears to have had a substantial impact on soil
productivity above Grutas Tzabnah.

In previous studies, investigators chose to analyse δ13Ccc as a regional palaeoclimate proxy,
instead of δ18Occ (17,27), given the disproportionate impact on δ18Occ values of tropical
cyclones (with highly negative δ18Orw and δ18Occ values) and changes in moisture source
(91). Our method of age modelling minimises the impact of these factors insofar as the prior
layer count ensures that significant negative excursions that occurred over a single year (e.g.,
from frequent summer cyclones) are not misinterpreted as multi-year wet periods. For
example, the δ18Occ excursion in 898 CE (fig. S1) likely represents a season of more frequent
or proximal cyclones amidst a drought, (and is within chronological error of the flooding
episode in 896 CE recorded by Frappier et al. (92)), not a prolonged return to wetter
conditions.

suggest that there were no significant changes in summer/winter moisture source throughout
the covered period. The (volumetric) majority of rain in northern

Mg/Ca in stalagmites is widely applied as an indicator of in-karst degassing and prior calcite
precipitation (PCP). Given that the degree of PCP will be higher when the karst is less
saturated, it can be used as a climate (precipitation) proxy on the timescale of karstic
infiltration. Stalagmite Mg/Ca is a robust indicator of PCP if the initial Mg/Ca in the
dripwater is constant overtime, there is little variation in the partition coefficient of Mg in
calcite, and the analysed Mg is precipitated in calcite and not attached to detrital materials.
Sr/Ca, while useful, is less robust as a PCP indicator, as the partition coefficient of Sr in
calcite may increase with increased growth rate or increasing Mg/Ca ratio (94-96).

To investigate these proxies in Tzab06-1, LA-ICP-MS analysis was conducted at Durham
University (Thermo Scientific X-Series2 (ICP-MS) coupled with a Teledyne Analyte
Excite+). Trace element ratios (cps/cps) for Mg/Ca and Sr/Ca were obtained as continuous
profiles (1-3 mm offset from the milled central axis) using a 285x12-µm rectangular slot at
10 µm s-1 and a 15-Hz laser repetition rate, resulting in 10-µm spatial resolution.

After removal of outliers, Tzab06-1 Mg/Ca varies around a mean of 8.2±1.8 (x10-3, 1σ), and
Sr/Ca varies around a mean of 0.41±0.05 (x10-3, 1σ), with little interannual variability (fig.
S10). Notably, strontium content, and the amplitude of variation, are sufficiently low to rule
out seasonal changes in mineralogy across laminae (calcite/aragonite) (95-98).

The extent of PCP was calculated to be small, and to vary less than ±10 % throughout the
period studied. Furthermore, in this low-variability range, there does not appear to be a strong
correlation between the amount of PCP and rainfall amount, as inferred from the δ18O record.
We are most confident in the stalagmite δ18O record interpretation, as interannual δ18O
variations are replicated in a second stalagmite from the site (15), interannual monitoring data
from 2014-2018 confirm wet-season droughts in the Yucatán are reflected in rainfall δ18O

(35,36) (fig. S7), and our initial monitoring at Grutas Tzabnah (2022-2023) demonstrates a
correlation between rainfall amount and drip water δ18O, with an average offset of one month
(Fig. 3). That we record apparent δ18O variability, but limited PCP variability, is consistent
with the environmental variables at this cave site. Grutas Tzabnah is overlain by thin
overburden (7 m) and little soil, with common exposure of surface bedrock, both of which
enable rapid transmission of rainwater and associated geochemical signals (i.e. δ18O) to the
cave but reduce the relative sensitivity of karst processes (i.e. PCP) to changes in rainfall. For
this reason, primary proxies (δ18O) are preferred to secondary proxies (δ13C, trace elements) at
this location as paleohydrology indicators.





S.7 Assignment of Droughts

Throughout the δ18Occ record, droughts were assigned when the minimum value (considered
the wettest extreme) within a given year did not drop below a given threshold for three or
more consecutive years (fig. S13). Conversely, a ‘wet period’ was assigned when the
minimum δ18Occ value within a given year did not rise above a given threshold for three or
more consecutive years. Both assignments were based on wet season extremes only, as this is
the metric that agricultural productivity most strongly responds to, with little regard for the
relative severity of dry seasons.

Fedick and Santiago (44) defined extreme droughts as ‘multiple years’ of skipped wet
seasons, we here increase this to three or more years. The thresholds are defined at 1σ above
and below the mean δ18O

dick and Santiago (44) defined extreme droughts as ‘multiple years’ of skipped wet
seasons, we here increase this to three or more years. The thresholds are defined at 1σ above
and below the mean δ18Occ record of the distribution of wet season extremes (fig. S14), such
that extreme droughts or wet events represent consecutive years outside the distribution’s 68
% interval. The resultant thresholds are -5.74 ‰ for droughts and -6.06 ‰ for wet periods.

Given that more of the time span of Tzab06-1 is characterised by droughts than wet periods,
the δ18O mean is higher than if the record were longer and included more ‘background
climate.’ Because of this, some marginal years not assigned as droughts here may reflect
drier-than-average conditions over longer timescales, and Tzab06-1 may underestimate the
long-term relative severity of the assigned droughts.

Example Analysis Script

The following script was used as part of data analysis in this study, originally run in Matlab
R2023a. The script is not required to replicate the data, and alternative software could be
used as appropriate. All data are provided in the Supplementary Tables accompanying this
article.

Example script for age calculation from U/Th

Excelinput = readtable('Table4.xlsx');
IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data = table2array(Excelinput);
date_measured = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,15); % date analysed on the MC-ICP-MS, CE.
U234_U238 = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,9); % 234U/238U ratio
Th230_U238 = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,11); % 230Th/238U ratio
Th232_U238 = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,13); % 232Th/238U ratio
U234_U238_1s = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,10); % 1σ for 234U/238U ratio
Th230_U238_1s = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,12); % 1σ for 230Th/238U ratio
Th232_U238_1s = IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data(:,14); % 1σ for 232Th/238U ratio

% initial 230Th/232Th atom ratio, calculated in Methods.
lowbound = 25e-6; % lower bound for initial 230Th/232Th atom ratio
upbound = 35e-6; % upper bound for initial 230Th/232Th atom ratio
Agestart = 1000; % starting value for fzero
n = 10000;
Lam238 = 1.55125E-10; %Cheng et al. 2013
Lam234 = 2.82206E-06; %Cheng et al. 2013
Lam230 = 9.1705E-06; %Cheng et al. 2013
Lam232 = 4.9475E-11; %Cheng et al. 2013
Th230_Th232_init_mc = unifrnd(lowbound,upbound,[n 1]).*(Lam230/Lam232);

U234_U238_mc = [];
Th230_U238_mc = [];
Th232_U238_mc = [];
[m,~] = size(IsoRatiosAgeEqn_data);
for i = 1:m
 U234_U238_mc(i,:) = U234_U238(i) + U234_U238_1s(i).*randn(1,n);
 Th230_U238_mc(i,:) = Th230_U238(i)

% outputs, all in years CE: uncorrected mean age, 95% interval lower, 95% interval
upper, corrected mean age, 95% interval lower, 95% interval upper, Initial 234U/238U
ratio, 95% interval lower, 95% interval upper
ages_final_CE = [];
for i = 1:m
 ages_final_CE(i,:) = [date_measured(i)-mean(Age_uncorr(i,:)) ...
 mean(Age_uncorr(i,:))-prctile(Age_uncorr(i,:),5) ...
 prctile(Age_uncorr(i,:),95)-mean(Age_uncorr(i,:)) ...
 date_measured(i)-mean(Age_corr(i,:)) ...
 mean(Age_corr(i,:))-prctile(Age_corr(i,:),5) ...
 prctile(Age_corr(i,:),95)-mean(Age_corr(i,:)) ...
 mean(U234_U238_init(i,:)) ...
 mean(U234_U238_init(i,:))-prctile(U234_U238_init(i,:),5) ...
 prctile(U234_U238_init(i,:),95)-mean(U234_U238_init(i,:))];
end

MANIOC CULTIVATION AT CEREN, EL SALVADOR:
OCCASIONAL KITCHEN GARDEN PLANT OR STAPLE
CROP?





Payson Sheets,a Christine Dixon,a Monica Guerra,b and Adam Blanforda
aDepartment of Anthropology, University of Colorado, Boulder CO 80309–0233
bDepartment of Geology, University of Colorado, Boulder CO 80309–0233

Abstract

Many scholars have thought the Classic period Maya did not cultivate the root crop manioc, while others have suggested it may have been
an occasional cultigen in kitchen gardens. For many decades there was no reliable evidence that the ancient Maya cultivated manioc, but in
the 1990s manioc pollen from the late Archaic was found in Belize, and somewhat older pollen was found in Tabasco. At about the same
time of those discoveries, research within the Ceren village, El Salvador, encountered occasional scattered manioc plants that had grown in
mounded ridges in kitchen gardens. These finds adjacent to households indicated manioc was not a staple crop, and vastly inferior to maize
and beans in food volume produced. However, 2007 research in an agricultural area 200 m south of the Ceren village encountered
intensive formal manioc planting beds. If manioc was widely cultivated in ancient times, its impressive productivity, ease of cultivation
even in poor soils, and drought resistance suggest it might have been a staple crop helping to support dense Maya populations in the

 A Cleared Area: Test Pits 3 & 4

 Test Pits 3 and 4 were excavated on top of the gently sloping hill
 south of the Ceren site. Both encountered a Classic period surface
 that had been largely cleared of vegetation, and had been tramped
 down and smoothed by considerable foot traffic and probably by
 a variety of human activities. Both test pit surfaces exhibited
 gentle ridges that had been almost eliminated by post-agricultural
 activities. The fact that the tops of the faint ridges were about
 115 cm apart indicates they were not the remains of a maize
 milpa. We believe it had been under manioc cultivation a few
 years before the eruption because that “wavelength” matches the
 manioc fields in Test Pits 1 and 2. A few weeds, two small
 bushes, and one small tree were encountered as hollow spaces and
 cast in dental plaster. The tree (Figure 7) had epiphytes growing
 on its lower trunk, only a few centimeters above the ground surface.

 We expected to find a diminution in productivity with distance
 from the Ceren village, because the care in field preparation and
 density of cultigens could decrease outside the settlement. More
 specifically, if we found maize, we expected to find less care in
 maize ridging, which could have taken the form of smaller ridges,
 or simpler mounding around a cluster of seeds sprouted into
 maize plants, or greater distances between ridge tops, or distances
 along the ridge tops where plantings were done. The actual results
 supported none of these, as intensity was the same as in the
 village. It was notable that maize had matured earlier within the
 village, whereas the maize discovered in Test Pits 5 and 6 needed
 another two or three weeks to mature. We think the most likely
 reason is that maize was planted earlier in the village, but it is poss-
 ible that greater organic returns (kitchen garbage and/or human
 waste) facilitated growth adjacent to households.

Reconstruction of precipitation changes in Central and South America during
the last 2000 years and the influence over civilizations

Juliano Henrique F. Soares



 ABSTRACT

Central and South America were scenario to some climate changes during the last two millennia. Changes in
precipitation were analysed from different sources and counter maps were made to show the evolution of
precipitation during the last 2000 years. These changes were responsible for many impacts in society and
ancient civilizations. In South America there was a drought around 200 AD responsible for an impact in Maya
civilization. They could recover themselves, and the cities that were abandoned started to be populated again.
However, about 900 AD bigger drought happened causing the entire collapse of Maya civilization. The Andean
civilizations were also influenced by precipitation changes. The Wari Empire, predecessor of Inca Empire, rose
in a drought conditions, which was responsible for a period of political conflict and warfare increase. The same
event was responsible for the Wari collapse some centuries later, once they could not sustain themselves in
such stressed conditions. After Wari collapse the Inca Empire started to rose in a period with humidity
conditions before 1400 AD. Afterwards the Inca Empire conquered large areas in west of South America and
became the biggest Empire in Pre-Colombian America. The modern world civilization is also modelled by
climate changes. The actual population is responsible for injecting anthropogenic aerosols into atmosphere,
which causes changes in tropical c

1. INTRODUCTION

Central and South America have been the scenario of many changes still not well studied. During the
last 2000 years the continent has passed through important climatic and anthropologic changes. The
climate has been changing between dry, wet, cold and warm, which has, directly or indirectly,
affected the people and civilizations that lived in the past. Relatively evolved civilizations has faced
their end probably for the influence of extreme climate conditions. These changes can have different
origins between natural or anthropic ones, and also can be periodic, with relatively frequent events
and cycles, or can be anomaly variation during a specific period of time.

Among all the civilizations that have lived in Pre-Colombian America, there were some with a
prominent position, which were the Maya and the Inca. These civilizations are recognized by their
evolved technology, the language, mathematics, astronomy and the complex writing for that time
(Katz, 1958; Lentz, 2014), once they lived before the arrival of Europeans in America. These people
have created huge civilizations and even empires. The Maya was a developed civilization, which lived
in Cent

958; Lentz, 2014), once they lived before the arrival of Europeans in America. These people
have created huge civilizations and even empires. The Maya was a developed civilization, which lived
in Central America, and the Inca was the biggest empire in pre-Colombian America, which lived in
the west coast of South America, in the region of Andes (Paulsen, 1976). All these civilizations have
probably suffered the influence of climate changes during the time they ruled territories in America.
Climate changes exerted influence on the rise of Wari Empire, predecessor of Inca Empire, and the
end of Maya, but it is possible that other factors are also related. All these civilizations have ended
before or when the European arrived at XVI century. The end of Maya civilization is still a mystery,
but several studies point the climate change as one of the main reasons ( Lachniet, et al, 2011; Haug

et al, 2003). Although the climate change has affected Inca Empire, they have ended by conflict with
the Europeans, when they have been conquered by the Spanish in the XVI century (Kolata, 2013).

Some natural and periodic climate events in atmosphere affect Central and South America, such as
the migration of the ITCZ. The ITCZ is a band that represents high moisture condition in atmosphere
that cross the Earth aligned with the east-west direction (Hess et al, 1993). It can be visualized from
space as a band of clouds in atmosphere and the regions below it is marked by intense precipitation
and moisture (Hess et al, 1993). The ITCZ controls the rainfall distribution in low latitudes and
changes with the season of the year influenced by the hemisphere temperature that drives the ITCZ
to the warmest hemisphere (Ridley et al, 2015). In present days it can achieve approximately 10°N
during the northern summer, and during the winter it is located over the equator or even southern
(Haug, 2001). However, there are factors that can change the position of ITCZ more radically. These
events happen through hundreds or thousands of years and change the average position of annual
ITCZ. The factors that can provide these changes in Earth surface can be the change of seasonality
insolation related to Milankovitch cycles, the El Niño events, which make the South America warmer,
driving the ITCZ to the south, surface conditions in Atlantic Ocean (Haug, 2001), and the injection of
greenhouse gases and aerosols into atmosphere (Ridley et al, 2015). These ITCZ variations can
change the rainfall

to the south, surface conditions in Atlantic Ocean (Haug, 2001), and the injection of
greenhouse gases and aerosols into atmosphere (Ridley et al, 2015). These ITCZ variations can
change the rainfall conditions in Central America and also around the world.

Differently from ITCZ movement, which regularly affects the America’s environment, anthropogenic
activities have changed the climate on Earth for some centuries. After 1800 the Industrial Revolution
have caused a great impact on Earth climate. Burning of fossil fuels has release lots of greenhouse
gases and aerosols that affected the Earth atmosphere (Ridley et al, 2015). The injection of these
substances has caused the decrease of precipitation in Central and South America and the
movement of ITCZ to the south, driving the continent to a drought, which started just after the
Industrial Revolution. The anthropogenic activities have cause the biggest impact in Earth
atmosphere in the last 2000 years.

Therefore, this paper will provide reconstruction of rainfall in Central and South America during the
last 2000 years based on datasets provided from different countries and different sources. It will
provide maps that show the evolution of rainfall in the continent and the changes in climate during
this period. It will also infer about the most important civilizations in the Pre-Colombian America and
how the climate change might have affected them. Afterwards, this paper will discuss the influence
that the industrialization has caused in Earth atmosphere and how the ITCZ behaved under this
influence.

2. METHODS

For starting this project it was necessary to make a bibliography research and collect data from
previous projects that have the approach over rainfall in any part of Central and South America. It
was collected numerical data from different papers that describe, in a way or another, the evolution
of precipitation in any point of the continent covering the last 2000 years. The papers were referent
to different places in the continent and were not correlated. The source of the data were also
different, including oxygen isotopes from foraminifera, titanium present in constitution of
speleothems, percentage of different grain sizes of sediments, grey scale and colours of lake
sediments and others. The location of each data and the article reference are described in Fig.1.
Once the nature of these sources is different, the numerical data and the interpretation of each one

are also different. Therefore, some process are necessary to analyse the data in an even way, and
minimize the difference between them.

To analyse the data and to correlate then in the same range, it was necessary to calculate the z-score
of each one. First it was calculated the average of each dataset, as well as the standard deviation.
The values of the z-score were calculated by each data value minus the average of all of them in one
dataset, and divided by the standard deviation. Once calculated every z-score, it is possible to
analyse all data in the same range of standard deviation, and them compare each dataset in an even
way. Since the numbers correspond the precipitation and the data have different origins, some
datasets correspond more rainfall in more positive values and others represent it with more
negative values. To correct this, some datasets were multiplied by minus one (-1) in a way that every
datasets correspond the same representation of rainfall.

After calculating the z-score, it was made the regular interpolation in the Past program, which
calculated the approximated values of each dataset separated by an interval of 50 years. This
method made it possible to compare the values of each dataset in specific years, and correlate the
values in a logical way. Therefore it was calculated the data from 1AD to 2000AD in intervals of 50
years.

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS

The maps made in Surfer program related to precipitation in Central and South America in the last
2000 years are summarized in Fig.2, which shows the evolution of rainfall with an interval
approximately of 250 years. In an overall view, these continents followed a trend in getting dryer
since the year 1 AD, with some variations during this period. Central America was wetter during the
first centuries, getting dryer between 500 and 1500 AD, and turning wetter again in the more recent
centuries. The South America has getting dryer in general, with some differences in the wettest
region of the continent. However, the evolution of precipitation is complex and dynamic, presenting
many changes and different patterns.

The intense climate change in Central and South America related to rainfall had influenced the
evolution of Pre-Colombian America native civilizations. It has contributed to rise and down of
cultures and empires. Therefore, this section will analyse and interpret the influence of climate
change in the ancient civilizations Maya and Inca.



3.1. MAYA

The Maya was a big civilization located in Central America that have occupied a region that today
corresponds to Yucatan Peninsula, Guatemala, Belize, parts of Southeast of Mexico and western
portion of Honduras and El Salvador (Coe, 2005). This region is represented in Fig.3 by the red line,
which delimits the Maya dominance. The Maya people have been, as well as much of the complex
civilizations in Pre-Colombian America, originated from the ancient Olmec civilization, which lived in
Centra

ich delimits the Maya dominance. The Maya people have been, as well as much of the complex
civilizations in Pre-Colombian America, originated from the ancient Olmec civilization, which lived in
Central America about 3000 year ago (Coe, 2005). The Maya cities and people were Extraordinary
cohesion and homogenous, which granted them a high security from invasion of other native tribes
(Coe, 2005).

The Maya civilization was, compared to other civilization, and even to European culture in some
points, very well evolved. The people had incredible architectural, astronomical, and artistic
achievement (Lentz, 2014). The cities were equipped with systems able to catch and store water
from the rainfalls, and also a good mechanism to distribute the water through the cities (Haug et al,
2003). Whoever, even though all this knowledge and technology were not able to avoid the great
collapse of the entire civilization.



3.1.1 PRE-CLASSIC COLLAPSE

The beginning of evolution of Maya civilization and culture was characterized as Pre-Classic period
that ended in the first collapse of the civilization. The Fig.3 represents the region that Maya
civilization has lived and the transition between a wetter phase before 200 AD to a drought that
culminate in the abandonment of many cities, passing through a peak in around 200 AD.

During the Pre-Classic period, when the weather conditions were favourable, the civilization has
grown in number of sites and in size of each site (Sharer, 2006). The population also grew up,
providing conditions to increase and centralization of political power, which

rable, the civilization has
grown in number of sites and in size of each site (Sharer, 2006). The population also grew up,
providing conditions to increase and centralization of political power, which was marked by building
of monumental temples, places, tombs, and carved monuments (Sharer, 2006). The good climate
and political conditions also provided the civilization the wealth and strength to lead them to
conquer large areas and populations, besides getting more trade routes with other civilizations
(Sharer, 2006).

However, the end of the Pre-Classic period, after 200 AD, was marked by a drought in Central
America, including the Maya dominance, as can be seen in Fig.3. During this event, several centres of
Maya civilization were abandoned, as example of Komchen, El Mirador, Cerros and mostly of
southern Maya area (Sharer, 2006). The causes of the abandonment and the collapse is still
uncertain and many students of the area discuss pointing different reasons (Sharer, 2006). In this
paper, it will be pointed the climate change as one of the main causes, however it is comprehensible
to have had other reasons that contributed to the collapse of Pre-Classical period in Maya history, as
political conflict and migration.

Sharer (2006), in his book, suggests that researches in El Salvador indicates an eruption of the
Ilopango volcano in the end of Pre-Classic period. The epoch of the eruption is not completely
defined, but it could be one cause of the collapse and abandonment of some areas (Sharer, 2006).
However, the eruption theory in not contradictory to the climate drought. As said in the
introduction, the volcanos eruptions can release aerosols, which can move the ITCZ position and
cause climate change (Ridley et al, 2015). Therefore it is possible that Ilopango volcano eruption has
changed the climate, provoking dryer conditions in the Maya region.

Releasing aerosols into the North hemisphere atmosphere, by volcano or anthropic factors, causes
the southern movement of the ITCZ (Ridley et al, 2015). Since the ITCZ is the most important source
of rainfall in Central America, its movemen

here atmosphere, by volcano or anthropic factors, causes
the southern movement of the ITCZ (Ridley et al, 2015). Since the ITCZ is the most important source
of rainfall in Central America, its movement to the south can drive the regions to dryer conditions as
can be interpreted from Fig.3. In the year 150 AD, which consist in the good environment for Maya
development, it can be seen that the northern Central America, and Maya dominance, is much
wetter, marked by intense blue colour. The southern Central America and the extreme northwest of
South America is marked by soft blue colour, which indicate a dryer condition, compared to the
more intense in Mexico area. These conditions can be attributed to the north position of ITZC,
causing more heavy rainfall in northern lands. After 150 AD, and especially in the peak of the
drought event around 200 AD, it is possible to see that the northwest of South America and
southern Central America is marked by a more intense blue colour, indicating a wetter condition and
also the southern position of ITCZ. The ITCZ movement to the south has caused the drought event in
Maya region and was probably caused, or at least influenced, by the injection of aerosols in North
hemisphere by the Ilopango volcano.

3.1.2 CLASSIC COLLAPSE

The Terminal Classic Period consist in the collapse of Maya civilization and is comprehended
between 700 to 950 AD (Haug et al, 2003). During this interval, a big drought event happened in the
Central America, especially in the dominance of Maya civilization (Fig.4). This event was much longer
that that one responsible for the Pre-Classic Collapse, and provoked the end of the entire civilization.
The drought has caused much influence in the civilization behaviours and production of food, which
affected directly the life of population, causing abandonment and the end of Maya civilization during
the ninth and tenth century.

The places that have been abandoned during the Pre-Classic Maya collapse, were reoccupied and
the civilization started to grow again after the weather conditions returned to be favourable.
However, the land that Maya civilization occupied did not provided much resources to development
of the civilization. The lowlands, region occupied by the Maya people, had few and sparse essential
sources, besides a redundant environment in matter of natural resources (Rathje, 1971). Because of
that it is presumed that the Maya people have developed knowledge and skills before occupying this
land, to being able to extract the basic sources (Dumond, 1961). Moreover, the transportation of
goods was difficult, because of the sparse sources and conditions of the land (Rathje, 1971). For
these difficulties, the resources could not achieve all the households equally, creating a scenario that
the goods were mostly concentrated in few hands (Rathje, 1971

the goods were mostly concentrated in few hands (Rathje, 1971).

Even though the conditions of the land that Maya civilization has developed was not the best in
matter of abundance and access of natural resources, the civilization became one of the biggest and
the most evolved and sophisticated culture during favourable climate conditions. In its peak around
700 AD, it is estimated that the Maya lowland had a population growth from 3 to 13 million
inhabitants (Haug et al, 2003). This popular expansion happened during a climate favourable,
comprehended between 550 and 750 AD, which has been characterized by relatively wetter
conditions that drove the number of people to the limit of the environment carrying capacity (Haug
et al, 2003). This interval is partially demonstrated in Fig.4, which shows the year of 650 and also 700
AD in wetter conditions, characterized by the more intense blue colour. From 750 AD to forward, the
conditions started to get dryer, characterizing the Terminal Classic Maya.

The agriculture was one of the bases of the Maya civilization, responsible to sustain the population.
However, the civilization has developed in a seasonal desert, condition that the agricultural
production could only be supported by a consistent rainfall cycle (Haug et al, 2003). The agriculture
was mainly based in slash-and-burn technique, which causes an intense decline of soil fertility due to
large production (Adams, 1973). During the good

was mainly based in slash-and-burn technique, which causes an intense decline of soil fertility due to
large production (Adams, 1973). During the good weather conditions, before the Classic Collapse,
when the population and wealth used to grow more and more, the agricultural production needed
to follow the population demand. Then, the utilization of the soil for slash-and-burn crop was
responsible for intense lack of fertility and nutrients of the following years, coinciding with the big
drought event that started around 750 AD (Adams, 1973). Therefore, the dryer conditions and the
misuse of the soil contributed to the abandon of cities and collapse of the civilization.

As the Maya people lived in an area characterized by seasonal rain, which started in May and
continue until November, the rest of the year were marked by a dry season, which there were some
sporadic and undependable rains (Culbert, 1973). The access to groundwater was scarce and
difficult, so precipitation was the main source of water for Maya civilization (Haug et al, 2003).
During the dry season in lowland, the few rainfalls were not sufficient either for agriculture or for

human’s personal necessities (Culbert, 1973). So, the Maya civilization developed technology and
strategies in engineering to store the water in reservoirs, which could be used during the months
with low precipitation. The Maya cities were equipped with systems able to collect and stores water
from rainfalls, besides building the cities in topographic highs to use the hydraulic gradient to
distribute the water through households and irrigation systems (Haug et al, 2003). Therefore, it is
easy to presume that the Mayas lived in a situation that any instability in the rainfall cycles would
affect directly the production and the life of people living in lowlands.

It is reasonable to affirm that the drought event played an important role in Classic Maya Collapse.
Given the civilization’s conditions, it is possible to say that they were quite dependent of the
seasonal rainfall and any variation of it would disturb the whole structure of the civilization. Haug et
al (2003) affirms that the Terminal Classic Maya happened between 750 and 950 AD. Lachniet, et al
(2011) splits this event in two pulses, between 770 and 870 AD and 920-1100 AD. Whichever the
period of Maya’s collapse, the drought event demonstrated in Fig.4, and also described by Coe
(2005), occurred between around 750 and 1050 AD. Coe (2005) also affirms it was one of the driest
interval recorded within the past three millennia and half. This event had such an impact in Maya
civilization that artefacts of the “Storm God” of Maya culture were found completely smashed,

The extraction and increasing of agricultural areas in Maya lowlands might have caused influence in
the environment in Yucatan Peninsula. Lake sediments suggest that 60-70% of forests in Maya
lowlands were cleared for extraction and utilization by Maya population during the Late Classic
period (Lentz, 2014). It is also estimated that about 32% of Bajo lands were deforested for the
utilization of the area to agriculture. Such removal of forest area and environmental degradation
could affect the local climate. Once a big percentage of precipitation is originated by forest
transpiration, if you remove the vegetation there will be less water vapour into atmosphere and also
a decrease of rainfall. This fact can be attributed to a local climate change, but does not explain the
big drought event that happened in whole Central America.

3.2 INCA EMPIRE

The Inca civilization was the biggest one in the Pre-Colombian America (Chepstow-Lusty et al 2009).
It was a big empire that controlled an area that covered most of west coast of South America, going
from a small part in southwest of Colombia to the centre of Chile, passing through Ecuador, Peru,
Bolivia and Argentina. In Fig.5 the Inca dominance is delimited by red lines. The pink lines
correspond to the same area, but before the consolidation of Inca Empire. The Inca Empire
established and ruled from about 1400 to 1532, when the Spanish caravans went to America and
destroyed the whole Empire (Paulsen, 1976; Kolata, 2013). However, the consolidation of Inca
Empire came from different political and climatic scenario. The climate change has rolled the rise
and down of predecessor civilizations that influenced and gave origin to Inca. The dominance and
development of the Inca Empire also were influenced by changes in precipitation.

Before 600 AD, long before the rises of Inca Empire, there was a pluvial period, which characterized
the west of South America with relatively intense precipitation (Paulsen, 1976). During this interval
the cultivation technics and agriculture have increased considerably, achieving lands that have never
been cultivated before (Paulsen, 1976). The farming production raised as consequence of the
intense precipitation and the development of slop-farming technics, which enabled the rise of
population in Andes territory (Paulsen, 1976). This situation can easily be seen in Fig.5-550 AD,
which represents the heavier rainfall by the intense blue colour in most of South America coast, with
a peak in the region that nowadays in localized Peru. However this situation changed in the next
centuries, and the cultivated lands start to diminish after about 600 AD, preceding a drought event
that took the Andean coast (Paulsen, 1976).

After about 600 AD climate starts to be dryer, driving the Andean region in a drought event that took

pressure of climate change over populations has aggravated the conflicts between tribes and
political interaction, which developed in increasing of warfare around this region and conquer of
new regions and other people (Paulsen, 1976). During this scenario, Wari and Tiwanauku people got
the opportunity and found the conditions to conquer other people and became empires in Andean
region, existing between 600 AD until around 1000 AD (Chepstow-Lusty et al 2009). It is notable the
difference in how the Maya civilization and Andean Empires responded in a different way the drier
conditions. Different from Maya, that has collapsed during a drought event in Central America, the
Andean empires found it a scenario to conquer other people and raise the autonomy and influence
through the intense warfare happening in the region.

However, a dry condition has much more a bad impact over civilizations than provide an opportunity
to increase, and even the Andean Empires couldn’t sustain the civilization in stressed environment
and have declined due to drought that happened between 600 and 1100 AD. The deteriorating
climate has affected the civilizations reducing the agricultural production and causing abandonment

3.3 INDUSTRIALIZATION

Around 1800 industrialization started to increase in many parts of the world, especially in Europe. In
this time, the humankind started to influence and interfere in the atmosphere and climate in a way
never seen before. Many gases and aerosols were injected into the atmosphere as results of
industrialization and extraction of natural resources in great scale. This practice caused some
changes in the environment and climate. As can be seen in Fig.6, since 1800 South America presents
an extreme dry conditions, showing features not seen in the last 2000 years maps. According to
Paulsen (1976), in Santa Elena Peninsula, the drought caused a decrease in precipitation from 500 to
80 mm, and in 1960s it was so dry that the water needed to be hauled by truck and sold in the cities.
Conditions that a prehistoric civilization could not survive.

Aerosols in atmosphere has a big impact in precipitation and can have different sources. It can be a
natural widespread source on surface as oceans and deserts, can be punctual as volcanos, and
spatial as clouds (Jaenicke, 1993). Aerosols are transported in atmosphere by turbulence and air
mass dislocation, and are removed by precipitation, coagulation, and sedimentation (Jaenicke,
1993). It plays a natural role in atmosphere, controlling the incidence of solar radiation on Earth’s
surface, rainfall distribution and maintenance of the climate as we know (Jaenicke, 1993). However,
the source that will be discussed in this section is the anthropogenic one, and the disorder it

th’s
surface, rainfall distribution and maintenance of the climate as we know (Jaenicke, 1993). However,
the source that will be discussed in this section is the anthropogenic one, and the disorder it causes
in Earth climate and natural conditions of the environment.

The increase of anthropogenic aerosols in atmosphere causes intense changes in tropical circulation
and reduction of precipitation (Rotstayn and Lohmann, 2002). In the same time that aerosols reduce
the solar radiation that achieve the surface, causing a decrease of temperature, it can cause heating
in atmosphere by elevated absorbing aerosols (Andreae and Rosenfeld, 2008). This process might
cause reduction of thermal convection and also of rainfall. The rainfall occurs due to condensation of
supersaturated water vapour on aerosols particles forming “cloud condensation nuclei” (CCN). The
CCN forms cloud droplets that precipitates as raindrops when achieve a considerable size. In an
atmosphere with high concentration of aerosols particles and then a high number of CCN, the
droplets are smaller and need much more water vapour to conglutinate in raindrops. The
consequence of this is ceasing rainfalls from shallow and short-lived clouds (Andreae and Rosenfeld,

2008). When low concentration of CCN, more rapidly the rainfalls are formed, and when higher
concentration of CCN, it takes longer to the cloud create rainfall, or it just may not happens.
Therefore, the injection of aerosols into atmosphere causes intense drop of rainfall.

The emission of anthropogenic aerosols is more concentrated in industrialized regions as Europe and
North America (Watson et al, 1990). Industrial process is one of the biggest causes of anthropogenic
aerosols emission and have increased through the last centuries. The dry condition in Central and
South America represented in Fig.6 started around 1800, when occurred the Industrial Revolution,
responsible for the intense increase of industrialization in Europe. Since this event the aerosols
emission has more than doubled, changing the climate (Watson et al, 1990). It has consequences

around the whole world and caused the drought in America during the last centuries (Fig.6). It is not
clear that aerosol emission was the only reason for this drought, but was probably one of the main

The increase of aerosols in atmosphere does not cause just the decrease of rainfall, but also the
variation in the position of the ITCZ (Ridley et al, 2015). Ridley et al (2015) also suggests that the
drought event since 1800 was characterized by the movement of ITCZ to the south and had
anthropogenic causes. The injection of aerosols in northern hemisphere drives the ITCZ to a
southern position, and also decreases the precipitation. Similar situation was identified in sediment
records when a large Northern Hemisphere volcanic eruption occurred releasing aerosols to the
atmosphere. This description agrees with the America pluvial maps in Fig.6, which show the
evolution of rainfall since 1800. According to the maps, there was as intense drought in southern
Central America and in northern South America between 1800 and 1950, region normally influenced
by ITCZ. The intense drought particularly in this point suggests a variation in the position of the
Intertropical Convergence Zone to the south.

However, this condition changed in 1990 when southern Central America and northern South
America presented a more humid condition again (Fig.6). It may have been a consequence of the
reduction of aerosol emission into atmosphere and the northern movement of ITCZ. In 1970 a clean
air regulation was established and the emission of aerosols started to be controlled and reduced

4. IMPLICATIONS

Drought events in Central and South America have caused different impacts in the Pre-Colombian
civilizations. The drought events that happened in Central America around 200 AD and 900 AD have
caused collapse and abandonment of many cities of Maya civilization. The latter one was responsible
for the end of the entire civilization that was relatively evolved and enjoyed prosperity during
climate favourable conditions. For the Andean civilizations drought events caused increase of
warfare, which culminated in the rise Wari Empire around 600 AD. According to Paulsen (1976), the
drought that happened in Santa Elena Peninsula also influenced the rise of Inca Empire by increasing
warfare and conquest of different areas. Therefore it is notable who different civilizations
correspond differently in stressed climate conditions. However, the drought that rose

warfare and conquest of different areas. Therefore it is notable who different civilizations
correspond differently in stressed climate conditions. However, the drought that rose the Wari
Empire was also responsible for its end some centuries later, because of the bad climate conditions.
The Inca Empire just was able to increase to the point to become the biggest one in Pre-Colombian
America because it ruled regions with intense precipitation, which was able to produce food to
sustain the increasing population.

The humankind has the power to change and affect directly the climate on Earth. The driest scenario
during the last 2000 years started after 1800, when the civilization in development started the
intense industrialization. Processes involving industrial advance were responsible for the injection of
different gases and aerosols into atmosphere. This anthropogenic gases and aerosols were
responsible for the reduction of precipitation and the southern movement of ITCZ, causing reduction

of rainfall in many areas. The Maya people also have affected the climate, but in a smaller scale.
They extract too much from the soil and removed large forest areas for natural resources and
agriculture. This might have influenced the climate in Maya dominance and was responsible for the
stress on civilization, which together with the drought, was responsible for the great collapse of
Maya. Therefore, there is no doubt that humans can affect and change the climate by environmental
impacts, and these changes can cause a stress conditions and several consequences to any
civilization.

Climate changes have caused great impact in ancient civilizations, and still can cause it in present
days. The decreasing of precipitation has caused the collapse of cultures and civilizations, and even
the end of Empires in Pre-Colombian America. Today we have technics and processes that allow us
to live in conditions that have collapsed ancient civilizations. However, the climate changes that
humans are causing is getting bigger, affecting every civilization in a global scale. Even though our
technics have evolved to support stressed environments, we still can be affected by huge climate
changes. We already know we are able to such change, and we know it can affect and destroy
populations. If we do not care about it, it is possible that the world population may face a climate
impact which causes much harm to our cultures and civilizations.

However, the climate impact we have caused can be corrected and futures changes can be avoid.

In the path of the Maize God: a royal
tomb at Nakum, Pet´en, Guatemala
Jarosław ´Zrałka1, Wiesław Koszkul1, Simon Martin2 &
Bernard Hermes3


 The authors describe the excavation and
 interpretation of an intact seventh-century
 high status burial at the Maya site of Nakum.
 The dead person wore an incised pectoral with
 an eventful biography, having started out as
 an Olmec heirloom 1000 years before. No less
 impressive was the series of votive rituals found
 to have been enacted at the tomb for another
 100 years or more. The beautiful objects, their
 architectural setting and the long story they
 recount, offer a heart-breaking indictment of
 the multiple losses due to looting.

jade, spindle whorls


Introduction

Intensive looting in ancient Maya cities has resulted in a tremendous loss of archaeological
information. The search for marketable artefacts from tombs and ritual deposits has damaged
or destroyed architecture directly, while the pits and trenches left by illicit excavations have
hastened the collapse of already fragile remains. North-eastern Guatemala has suffered
greatly from this devastation. At the large site of Naranjo, for example, the two looter’s

Nakum: history of investigations and description of the site

Nakum lies at an elevation of about 200m asl and is situated in the heart of the modern
Guatemalan district of Pet´en. Its discovery is attributed to the French Count Maurice de
P´erigny in 1905; who returned to explore the ruins in 1910 (P´erigny 1908, 1911). Further
reconnaissance was carried out by Alfred Tozzer and Raymond Merwin from the Peabody
Museum, Harvard University (Tozzer 1913) and later by Sylvanus Morley (1937–38) and
Nicholas Hellmuth (1992). In 1989, IDAEH initiated efforts

out by Alfred Tozzer and Raymond Merwin from the Peabody
Museum, Harvard University (Tozzer 1913) and later by Sylvanus Morley (1937–38) and
Nicholas Hellmuth (1992). In 1989, IDAEH initiated efforts to rescue and protect buildings
in the core area of the site. Formal investigations were initiated in 1994 with the restoration
and excavation of the most deteriorated monumental structures in the southern sector of
the site.
 IDEAH investigations indicate Nakum was ﬁrst settled during the Middle Preclassic
period (c. 800–300 BC). Many structures visible at Nakum today were constructed in the
Late Classic period (AD 600–800) — the apogee of Maya civilisation. However, one of the
most intriguing features of Nakum is its vigorous development during the Terminal Classic
period (ninth–tenth centuries AD), when most other Southern Lowland Maya centres were
in decline (Hermes & ´Zrałka 2008). The core of Nakum is divided into northern and
southern sectors connected by the P´erigny Causeway, named after the discoverer of the
ruins. The largest and most impressive is the southern sector which is home to several tall
temple-pyramid structures (Structures A, B, C, V and U) as well as the extensive Acropolis
complex and many other buildings. The Acropolis (Figure 1) consists of a large platform,
180×150m at its base, which is topped primarily by ‘palace-like’ structures grouped around
12 courtyards or patios.

Grave goods: pottery

Three vessels were deposited in the southern part of the tomb chamber (Figure 5). Two
of them were large monochrome bowls of the Azucar Impressed (Vessel 1) and Chaquiste

ﬂange tripod plate with semi-cylindrical supports. It held the skeleton of a bird and several
small pieces of charcoal. Painted at the centre of this plate was a representation of the
dancing Maize God, one of the most important deities for the ancient Maya. This vessel
can be ascribed to the so-called ‘Tikal Dancer’ style (see: Re

 One explanation is that it was kept by the royal family as an heirloom and deposited in
the burial of a much later dynast. This was a popular custom among the ancient Maya and
we know of several other royal tombs in which items from earlier times were included (e.g.
at Calakmul [see: Carrasco 1998: 384; Fields & Reents-Budet 2005: 255] or Palenque [Ruz
1973: ﬁg. 226]). The ancient Maya sometimes acquired and kept objects of even greater
antiquity, made in Olmec style (e.g. pectorals and pendants), which in some cases werecovered by new inscriptions and representations (Schele & Miller 1986: 119–20; Fields & Research
Reents-Budet 2005: 182, 191–4; see also Pellecer Alecio 2006: 1028; Freidel 2010). Such
objects, related to real or ﬁctitious ancestors, served to legitimise the power of the kings
who possessed them. The Nakum pectoral is clearly related to much earlier jade ornaments
attributed to the Olmec culture, were they are often referred to as ‘spoons’ or ‘clamshell

98). The close resemblance of the Nakum pectoral to several similar Olmec artefacts may
indicate that it is actually an Olmec piece that was subsequently reused by the Maya who
made incisions on both sides of it. Moreover, the suspension holes drilled in the Nakum

Spindle whorls and sex

Among the other artefacts found in Burial 1 were four spindle whorls (Figure 8). Weaving
was an important activity for Maya women, even among the elite, and the discovery of
spindle whorls as well as a small ﬁnger ring (sized appropriately for a female hand) in the
tomb could indicate that it held a royal woman. Most lowland Maya burials containing
spindle whorls and where the sex could be determined, belonged to women, especially at the
aforementioned neighbours of Nakum, Tikal and Uaxactun (Welsh 1988), as well as at more
distant Caracol (Chase et al. 2008). That said, spindle whorls have also been documented
in male burials from the south-eastern Pet´en, the Guatemalan Paciﬁc coast and adjacent
highlands (Chase et al. 2008: 136; Cossich 2009). Moreover, it is known that weaving
was performed by men in colonial and modern times in both the Maya highlands and in
Central Mexico (Cossich pers. comm. 2008; Cossich 2009). The available data indicates
that although spindle whor

ing
was performed by men in colonial and modern times in both the Maya highlands and in
Central Mexico (Cossich pers. comm. 2008; Cossich 2009). The available data indicates
that although spindle whorls predominate in female burials, they are not secure pointers
to the sex of the interred. The signiﬁcance of their deposition may have less to do with
craft specialisation and the tasks of daily life than with religious symbolism. Among the
contemporary Tz’utujil Maya, the process of weaving is conceived in terms akin to the
process of birth. Similar concepts can also be detected in pre-Columbian Central Mexico,
where spinning and weaving were metaphors for life, death and rebirth (Sullivan 1982;
Koszkul et al. 2009).

Offerings for the royal person and the Protoclassic burial

The temple-style building located at the summit (phase 15–1) originally had two
interconnected rooms. The Maya reused the western one for Burial 1, while the eastern
chamber received associated offerings (Figure 9). The ﬁrst offering (no. 11) consisted
of a group of 27 limestone bars carefully deposited in a small cavity cut into the ﬂoor
(Figure 10). The precise function of these bars is unknown, although some have suggested
that similar objects might have been used as spacers in the production of ﬁshing nets or
some other kind of weaving technology (Chase et al. 2008: 133). The second offering (no.
12) from the same chamber included two large ceramic plates, one of which was upturned
and covering the other — enclosed between them was a small jade bead (Figure 10). Close
to these vessels were found nine ﬂint knives and projectile points (Figure 11), some in a
vertical position others beneath the plates. At least four of the ﬂints were stuccoed and
painted with a blue pigment that was well preserved. After these depositions were made, the
eastern room was ﬁlled with rubble and both chambers were sealed by the construction of a
surmounting ﬂoor. This new level was topped by a building that was made almost entirely
from perishable materials.

At about 5m another interment was encountered. Burial 2 consisted of a crypt lined and

was furnished with two polychrome vessels and a shell bead. Stratigraphically, the crypt was
associated with an earlier version of Structure 15 (phase 15 Sub-1). It was most probably
placed into the substructure after the death of an important member of the local elite.
Both vessels deposited in the burial represent the Ixcanrio Orange Polychrome type and are
typical of the still poorly understood Protoclassic phase (c. 100/50 BC–AD 250/300+).
The location of Nakum Burial 2, the style of its construction, and furnishings, suggest that
it was an elite burial, probably for another member of the local royal family.


Discussion

We identify Burial 1 as that of a Nakum ruler, based on a number of factors. Analysis of
Preclassic and Classic lowland Maya burials made by Krejci and Culbert (1995) shows that
a special category of burials belonging to the uppermost class of Maya society and classiﬁed
as ‘royal burials’ can be distinguished by their size, their el

ade by Krejci and Culbert (1995) shows that
a special category of burials belonging to the uppermost class of Maya society and classiﬁed
as ‘royal burials’ can be distinguished by their size, their elaborate contents and their central
location. The authors give a number of status markers of these royal tombs (Krejci & Culbert
1995: tab. 11), the most important of which are present in the Nakum case. These include
its formal construction within a large structure of pyramid-temple type, its orientation on
the central axis of the building, and the enormous size of its interior space (one of the largest
yet found in the Maya lowlands). Moreover, Structure 15 is located in the Acropolis — the
largest and most impressive complex of Nakum. Among other status markers of royal burials
present in Burial 1 is the large quantity of precious objects — including ear spools — and a
red pigment that once covered the body. Of special importance is the large number of jade
and shell artefacts, foremost among them a unique jade pectoral.
 The discoveries of major interments and ritual offerings inside Structure 15, spanning
several hundred years, demonstrates that this building had an enduring signiﬁcance for the

inhabitants. Structure 15’s location on the eastern side of Patio 1 — the largest courtyard of
the huge Acropolis complex — makes it part of a wider pattern in elite Maya burials. Given
its royal associations, Nakum Structure 15 may well have functioned, for at least part of its
existence, as a memorial for the local ruling family.

 It has long been recognised that jade jewellery had a meaning beyond its intrinsic value
and role in personal beautiﬁcation. Jade jewels were the ﬁnery of the Maize God, the green
colour symbolic of the green foliage of sprouting cornstalks (Miller & Martin 2004: 70;
Taube 2005). Maya kings believed that after death they would follow the path of the Maize
God, defeat the Lords of Death in the Underworld and be reborn. In preparation for this
resurrection they were dressed for their last journey in the ceremonial jewellery that they had
worn during their lives (Miller & Martin 2004: 57–8, 70). The Tikal Dancer plate provides
an explicit link to the mythology of the Maya Maize God. The subject of such plates is the
dance of resurrection and apotheosis for the Maize God (Reents-Budet 1994: 198; Looper
et al. 2009: 124). It refers to the moment when this deity ﬁrst dances and then ascends into
the sky, indicated by his dynamic pose and elements such as the feathered wings sometimes
shown on his arms or belt (Looper et al. 2009: 124). In Nakum, this theme of rebirth and
ascension may be further symbolised by the presence of the skeleton of a bird deposited
inside the Tikal Dancer plate.

In the path of the Maize God

 In sum, the evidence recovered by the excavation of Burial 1 in Nakum Structure 15
permits a series of deductions and inferences. We may surmise that it contained an important
local dynast who, in accordance with the Maya world-view and beliefs, was believed to have
entered the path of the Maize God — a journey of transformation that promised rebirth
both in the twin metaphors of a recurring harvest of corn and in the daily rising of the sun
at dawn.

From E-Group to Funerary Pyramid: Mortuary Cults and
 Ancestor Veneration in the Maya Centre of Nakum, Petén,
 Guatemala


 Jarosław ´Zrałka, Wiesław Koszkul, Bernard Hermes,
 Juan Luis Velásquez, Varinia Matute & Bogumił Pilarski


 Recent investigations at the Maya centre of Nakum (in Guatemala) enabled the study of the
 evolution of an interesting complex of buildings that started as the so-called E-Group, built
 during the Preclassic period (c. 600–300 BC). It was used for solar observations and rituals
 commemorating agricultural and calendrical cycles. During the Classic period (AD 250–
 800), the major building of the complex (Structure X) was converted into a large pyramidal
 temple where several burials, including at least one royal tomb, were placed. We were also
 able to document evidence of mortuary cults conducted by the Maya in the temple building
 situated above the burials. The architectural conversion documented in Structure X may re-
 flect important religious and social changes: a transformation from the place where the Sun
 was observed and worshipped to the place where deceased and deified kings were apotheo-
 sized as the Sun Deity during the Classic. Thus the Maya transformed Structure X into
 one of the most sacred loci at Nakum by imbuing it with a complex solar and underworld
 symbolism and associating it with the cult of deified ancestors.

Introduction

The pre-Columbian Maya, like many other civilisations of the ancient world, ﬂourished
in an area highly dependent on access to water sources or water-related features. During
the rainy season, the excess of water must have been channelled out of the Maya cities or
architectural complexes to avoid ﬂooding. Meanwhile, in dry seasons people might have
suffered due to the lack of rain if water had not been stored previously in special reservoirs
constructed by the Maya. The control of water was a crucial issue in the life of every Maya
community. The Maya constructed special water-related features that had practical functions
and were also used to strengthen the power of local lords who could

The Nakum site

Nakum consists of two separate architectural sectors (northern and southern) located on two
low natural hills in the close vicinity of the Holmul River. Both sectors are connected by an
elevated causeway (the P´erigny Causeway), which is approximately 250m long × 26m wide.

Discussion and conclusions

The management of water was a very important aspect of Maya daily life and ritual.
Almost every site had a system to collect water run-off, from architectural buildings to
special reservoirs or other catchment systems (Fash & Davis-Salazar 2006: 130). The Maya
modiﬁed the landscape and designed their building programmes with the intention of

draining their cities and particular complexes, and canalising the water to exterior areas and
collecting the runoff in aguadas, chultuns (usually bottle-like, artiﬁcial features dug into the
bedrock) and other reservoirs (Lentz et al. 2010; Akpinar Ferrand et al. 2012; Scarborough
et al. 2012; Seefeld 2013; Weiss-Krejci 2013). Many, if not most, structures, patios and
plazas were designed to direct rainwater run-off in a particular direction. Terraces in every
structure had slight slopes for that purpose that directed water down to the patios and plazas.The ﬂoors of the plazas also had appropriate declinations to drain rainwater outside the Research
building, architectonic complex or city. Moreover, the ancient Maya applied many different
drainage and ﬂood-control constructions such as aqueducts, channels, drains, substructures
or subterranean conduits, dams and other devices (see Davis-Salazar 2006; French et al.
2006; Lucero & Fash 2006; French 2007).
 As many studies have shown, the management of water also had ritual connotations
(Scarborough 1998; Fash 2005; Lucero 2006). It must be remembered that many
Mesoamerican sites or complexes were considered by the Maya as man-made replicas of
sacred landscapes. It is known that pyramids and other smaller buildings were viewed
as witz, or mountains (see Vogt & Stuart 2005). As mentioned above, in many cases
they were embellished with architectural sculptures (such as heads of witz monsters),
strongly indicating the underlying symbolism. On the other hand, courtyards located close
to pyramid

in many cases
they were embellished with architectural sculptures (such as heads of witz monsters),
strongly indicating the underlying symbolism. On the other hand, courtyards located close
to pyramids symbolised the waters of the underworld or the waters of creation (Freidel
et al. 1993: 139; Fash & Davis-Salazar 2006: 130). The water that ﬁlled patios during
the rainy season reinforced such symbolism. Moreover, pyramids surrounding courtyards
ﬁlled with water were considered to be ﬂoating symbolically on the primeval waters of
creation.
 The Nakum ﬁndings show water management features that are both functional and
ritual. The construction, which drained Patio 1 in the direction of the aguada, is a very
practical subterranean drain channel. Its function was both to drain the largest courtyard of
the enormous Acropolis complex and to carry rainwater to the neighbouring aguada where
it could be stored for a long time. Constructions similar in shape, dimensions and function
to the subﬂoor canal from the western part of the Nakum Acropolis were documented at
several other Maya sites (e.g. at Palenque, Copan or Piedras Negras) (see Davis-Salazar 2006;
French 2007; S. Houston pers. comm. 2014).

is unique in its sophistication and in having the rare trapezoidal element. We argue that
it was intended to symbolise a sacred mountain, in a manner similar to pyramids in most
other Maya sites. Running water, which encircled the ‘artiﬁcial mountain’, strengthened this
symbolism. Moreover, the water mount

its interior, constructed during the same architectural effort or stage as the drain, might have
symbolised an entrance to the mountain or, in other words, to the underworld. It may not
be coincidental that this space was used for rituals related to funerals or was perhaps a resting
place for one of the local lords. Maya lords, buried in tombs located within pyramids were
symbolically encapsulated in the realm of the underworld, an artiﬁcial cave hidden inside
the sacred mountain.

Ancient Maya water management

 Accessible archaeological data indicate that rituals and other types of activities connected
with Structure 14 and with the replica of a sacred mountain might have been meant to attract
and unify the local population through the ritual control of water and its sacred resources.
The fact that the Structure 14 feature was easily visible to the public from most of Patio 1
may indicate that it served to reinforce the power of the local elites. The trapezoidal feature
associated with the drain did not bear any associated iconography, but it was a functional
and visual object that showed water ﬂowing from the interior of the mountain. Based on
available archaeological data, we can assume that there must have been some construction
(possibly hidden) set up at the beginning of the Nakum drain that stored water, which
could be released during special events or ceremonies. Such events were supposed to show
the local rulers as lords of water and rainmakers who could control water and its sources;
thanks to them this beneﬁcial substance would come to the middle world and feed their
people. Since Olmec times, Mesoamerican iconography focused on showing rulers as the
Lords of Water, having the power to control water and rain (cf. Diehl 2004: 38–39; French
et al. 2006: 149–50; Houston 2010; Alvarado 2013). On many Maya carved monuments
(e.g. at Cancuen, Copan or Machaquila) we can see rulers associated with water-related
elements such as aquatic birds, ﬁsh, turtles, aquatic plants or water mountains shown in
zoomorphic form. Not only did such elements serve

r Machaquila) we can see rulers associated with water-related
elements such as aquatic birds, ﬁsh, turtles, aquatic plants or water mountains shown in
zoomorphic form. Not only did such elements serve as emblems of power, they also signalled
the divine abilities of rulers in controlling water sources as well as in providing fertility and
sustenance to their cities and populations. Rulers were also perceived as those who guarded
water and the reservoirs where it could be found (Fash 2005, 2010; Alvarado 2013). Maya
lords, representing themselves with water symbols on carved monuments, conducting water-
related rituals or constructing water-related features, showed that they were crucial in the
supplication of water and in keeping its balance during periods of both shortage and excess.
As such, the control of water and its sources might have been one of the fundamental issues
on which the power of Maya rulers was based and which enabled control over Maya society
(cf. Scarborough 1998; Lucero 2002, 2006; Fash 2005, 2010; Alvarado 2013).

SPECIAL ISSUE
 Art, Material Culture, Visual Culture, or Something Else

 ‘Art’ in Archaeology and Anthropology: An Overview of
 the Concept


 John Robb


 The concept of art has proved controversial in archaeology and anthropology. Many feel that
 the concept, developed to fit high art in modern Western society, is inappropriate for objects
 made for other uses, in other times, or in other cultures. Yet there is no widely agreed critique
 or alternative concept. This introduction reviews responses to this dilemma, ranging from
 using the concept uncritically, using the term ‘art’ simply as an archaeological convenience
 to refer to things such as petroglyphs and figurines, and treating art simply as material
 culture. It then explores the recent concepts of art as affective material culture, as socially
 defined networks, and as locally defined aesthetic action. Finally, it raises the possibility
 that art is our local category of the kind of powerful objects found in many cultures.

Kostas Vlassopoulos
Intercultural Relations and the Barbarian
Repertoire in Greek Culture

Abstract: The study of intercultural contacts in antiquity has been dominated by
two diametrically opposed approaches. The first one considers that intercultural
contacts are based on a relatively simple transfer of information, knowledge,
and objects from one culture to another. The second one, influenced by the
structuralist school of cultural anthropology, considers that intercultural con-
tacts are structured on the basis of polarity and, therefore, the images of other
cultures found in ancient Greek literature aim at constructing Greek identities
through the contrast with barbarian otherness, rather than transmitting real
knowledge about other cultures. My chapter aims to present a different ap-
proach to the topic. This approach is based on the realization that there are
radically different ways in which one culture may relate to other cultures. The
distinction between self-referential and hetero-referential cultures is necessary
for understanding the peculiar way in which ancient Greek culture relates to
other cultures. The construction of the “barbarian repertoire,” which includes a
multitude of different and often diametrically opposed images of other cultures,
and the diversity of those images’ uses, is one of the most peculiar and seminal
aspects of ancient Greek culture.

 The second peculiar aspect of Greek culture is the way it relates to cross-
cultural interactions and encounters. There should be no doubt that Persians,
Thracians, or Babylonians participated in intercultural communication and
reflected on it as much as the Greeks.27 This was a primarily oral universe in
which countless stories, customs, information, and ideas endlessly circulated.
The Greek peculiarity was the textualisation of this oral universe through the
development of literary genres which were based on the encounters and interac-
tions of the four parallel worlds and the processes of intercultural communica-
tion. Sailors from all societies developed stories and a stock of information
which was crucial for navigating in foreign lands and waters; what was peculiar
about the Greeks was the textualisation of this information and stories into a
literary genre, the Periploi, descriptions of foreign lands from a coastal perspec-
tive, which further developed into what we would describe as anthropology.
Stories about mercenary soldiers abroad must have been common among Car-
ian and Jewish mercenaries in Egypt; Greek authors textualised such stories in a
variety of literary genres. We find such stories in the historical works of Herodo-
tus and Ctesias; Xenophon used his own experience as a mercenary for a Per-
